explain.say: How can anyone know whether it will rain tomorrow? Nobody can see the future, but forecasters do the next best thing. Look at the first stage. Every hour, thousands of weather stations on land, ships and buoys measure temperature, wind, air pressure and rain.

explain.say: See the satellite? Weather balloons float up more than 20 kilometres, sending back measurements, and satellites watch clouds and storms from space. Together, these numbers show what the air is doing right now, all round the world. Why do you think they need the whole world?

explain.say: Look at the supercomputer. It splits the air around Earth into millions of boxes, like a giant 3D grid. Then, using the laws of physics, it works out how the air in each box will move, warm, cool and make clouds, step by step into the future.

explain.say: See the chip? The computer runs the forecast many times, each starting slightly differently. If most runs agree, the forecast is confident; if they spread out, it's less sure. Then, at the person, forecasters check it and write it up. Have you checked today's weather?

faq.q: Where does weather data come from?
faq.a: From thousands of weather stations, ships, buoys, aircraft, weather balloons and satellites, all sharing measurements around the world.
asks: How do they measure the weather?

faq.q: How does a computer predict the weather?
faq.a: It splits the atmosphere into millions of grid boxes and uses the laws of physics to calculate how air, heat and water in each box will change over time.

faq.q: What does an ensemble forecast mean?
faq.a: The computer runs the forecast many times with slightly different starting conditions. If the runs agree, forecasters are more confident.
asks: Why do forecasters run the model many times?

faq.a: The atmosphere is chaotic: tiny differences now can grow into big changes later. So forecasts are best for the next few days and less sure further ahead.
asks: Why can't they forecast weather weeks ahead?

faq.q: How far ahead can weather be forecast?
faq.a: Forecasts are usually useful for about a week. Beyond about two weeks, only general trends can be predicted.
asks: Can weather be predicted a month ahead?

facts: Weather balloons carrying instruments called radiosondes are launched twice a day from hundreds of sites worldwide.
In 1922 Lewis Fry Richardson imagined a forecast factory of 64,000 human computers.
